readerContract.humanQuestion: What changed in New York City schools, where does the generative-AI pause apply, and can school staff still use AI to make decisions about students?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: Understand the school-only, student-facing boundary; see the separate rules for high school, accessibility tools and staff use; and know what the current review process proves and does not prove.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: No knowledge of NYC school grades, generative AI, school procurement or ERMA is assumed.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: The policy draws separate boundaries around who is using AI, for what purpose, and with what kind of review: younger-student use is paused, high-school use is limited, accessibility tools remain, and staff cannot hand consequential student decisions to AI.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: A child in a reader’s family may be asked to use a school tool, receive a grade or placement decision, or rely on assistive or language-access technology.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A September 11 NewsStand report on the September 2 announcement as students returned September 10, using the current family guidance rather than the launch headline alone.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can tell what is actually prohibited at school, what remains allowed, and which claims about safety or learning are still unproven.

canonicalTruth.owner: NYC Mayor’s Office owns the September 2 announcement; NYC Public Schools owns the current policy and family notice; Associated Press owns its reporting and quoted reactions; NewsStand owns the bounded synthesis.
canonicalTruth.freshnessTrigger: Reopen the current NYCPS guidance, Mayor’s Office announcement and independent reporting if publication slips beyond September 11, the policy changes, the pilots begin reporting results, or the April 2027 coalition report appears.

strengthsToUse: Separate the headline rule from its exact scope
Place each evidence limit beside the claim it limits
End with the named route families can actually use
patternsNotToCopy: The source topic, metaphor or exact section wording

glossaryAccumulation.producerGuard: State the September 2 announcement and September 10 school return separately. Define student-facing generative AI before narrowing the pause to NYC public-school use in early-childhood programs through eighth grade. Preserve high-school pilots, accessibility and language exceptions, and the staff ban on AI grading, behavior monitoring and placement/promotion/graduation decisions. State that the current software-review process checks privacy and security; do not convert approved status into proven learning benefit, absence of bias or correct implementation at every school.
glossaryAccumulation.preventionEvidence: The planned story leads with the exact school-year scope, makes the user-purpose-review boundaries visible, places the current software-review limit beside pilot approval, and gives families the principal/SLT/CEC route named in current guidance.

candidateRepairPreflight.schoolBoundary: Say NYC public schools and student-facing use; do not imply a home, private-school or national ban.
candidateRepairPreflight.whoDoesWhat: Separate student use, high-school supervised pilots, assistive/language access and staff planning.
candidateRepairPreflight.consequentialDecisionRule: State the current staff prohibition on AI grading, behavior monitoring and student placement/promotion/graduation decisions.
candidateRepairPreflight.reviewLimit: ERMA currently covers privacy/security; bias, equity and instructional-effectiveness evaluation capacity is still being built.
candidateRepairPreflight.time: Keep September 2 announcement, September 10 return and April 2027 planned report distinct.
candidateRepairPreflight.independentContext: Attribute union and Fairplay concerns to AP’s quoted sources; do not convert them into findings.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: NYC Public Schools paused student-facing generative AI from early-childhood programs through eighth grade during the 2026–27 school year, limited high-school use to approved supervised programs, preserved necessary accessibility and language tools, and prohibited staff from using AI for consequential decisions about students.
causalSequence: The September 2 announcement set a one-year school policy before students returned September 10.
Student-facing generative AI is paused from early-childhood programs through eighth grade; high-school use is limited to approved supervised programs and AI literacy.
Necessary accessibility and language tools remain available.
Staff may use approved AI for planning and operations but not grading, behavior monitoring, placement, promotion, graduation or other student decisions.
The current software-review process covers privacy and security; NYCPS says broader bias, equity and instructional-effectiveness evaluation capacity is still being built.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A middle-school student should not be assigned a student-facing generative-AI tool under the moratorium. A teacher may use an approved AI tool for planning, but cannot let it assign the student’s grade or placement.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: For any school technology rule, ask who is using the tool, what decision it influences, and what the cited review actually tested.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: For a tool used at a child’s NYC public school, the current guidance names the school principal; concerns can also go to the school, School Leadership Team or Community Education Council.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: No broad anti-AI moral, national-ban framing, product list, screen-time detour or unsupported learning-benefit claim.

humourPlan.noneReason: The concrete school rule and grading boundary are memorable without humour.

explanationArc.adaptation: The event leads; who uses AI and what decision it touches provide the mechanism; the current review limit and named contact route provide the payoff.

discoveryChecks.question: Is generative AI banned for every NYC child everywhere?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. The reviewed policy governs NYC public-school use and student-facing generative AI for early-childhood programs through eighth grade during the 2026–27 school year.

discoveryChecks.question: Does the policy prohibit every use of AI by teachers?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. Approved planning and operational uses remain, while grading, behavior monitoring and consequential student decisions are prohibited.

discoveryChecks.question: Does ERMA approval prove a tool improves learning or is free of bias?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. NYCPS says the current software-review process checks privacy and security and broader evaluation capacity is still being built.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: A broad “AI ban” headline could erase high-school pilots, staff use and accessibility tools, while “vetted” could be mistaken for proven learning value.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: Write one exact scope sentence, one concrete student-versus-staff example and one ERMA-limit sentence before independent review.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: A reader can explain the younger-grade pause, high-school boundary, accessibility exception, staff decision prohibition and current review limit.
